pages.title: Accelerators
pages.note:
This is the demand engine's silicon — [[nvda]] plus the challengers. Little new standalone signal this week; the names mostly appeared inside the indiscriminate-selloff list ([[amd]] and peers down 4-10% in the Samsung-triggered rout), which [[aleabitoreddit]] reads as margin cascades rather than fundamentals. He treats [[nvda]] as the gravitational center rather than a pick — the edge is in the layers beneath it ([[photonics]], [[memory]], [[fabs]]).

[[amd]] is the merchant-GPU alternative; [[arm]] the architecture licensor riding the same compute wave. The desk's stance on the group is deliberately hands-off: express the view through the suppliers this map surfaces, not the headline chip.

pages.title: Fabs & Foundries
pages.note:
The desk took its first position in this layer's anchor. [[tsm]] moved to accumulate on 10 August — not because anything improved at the foundry, but because everything downstream got expensive. First-half revenue up 35.6% with June alone up 67.9%, monthly disclosure that lets the demand curve be checked continuously, and a share price down about 7% on the month while the [[photonics]] names it supplies ran 48-77%.

The layer's own bottleneck is loosening: industry reporting has the CoWoS advanced-packaging gap narrowing from roughly 20% to 10% by end-2026 as capacity expands toward about 200,000 wafers a month by end-2027. That is why TSMC is being held as ballast rather than as a squeeze trade, and why the scarcity thesis on this map keeps migrating upstream toward lasers, substrates and glass. [[gfs]] and [[intc]] are unchanged on watch; neither had new evidence this week.

pages.title: Glass Substrates
pages.note:
Glass-core substrates for [[advanced-packaging]] — a natural extension of the packaging wave as chips grow larger and run hotter, and still the thinnest layer on this map.

On 17 Aug 2026 the desk moved [[lpk-de]] here from [[materials]], where it had been filed as an equipment name, and gave it its first verdict. That makes two names in the layer alongside Corning (GLW), which has surfaced only inside broader semis-selloff baskets. SKC Absolics and TSMC's CoPoS effort remain tracked as candidates rather than positions.

The layer's problem this week is timing rather than technology. [[aleabitoreddit]] reported Samsung Electro-Mechanics delaying its glass-substrate investment on customer reliability-evaluation bottlenecks, revising the start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back — a delay in his own theme, which is the kind of disclosure worth weighting heavily precisely because it cuts against the poster's book. For an equipment supplier that pushes the revenue event out with it.

Glass stays a 2028-2029 layer on current evidence. Watch for the first disclosed tool order with a delivery year attached; that is what converts this page from a theme into a position.

pages.title: Hyperscalers
pages.note:
The hyperscalers are held here as the demand signal rather than as growth equities: if [[amzn]], [[googl]], [[meta]] and MSFT keep raising capex, the supply chain beneath them has a funded order book. Combined 2026 guidance moved to roughly $720-745bn from $695-725bn during late July 2026, with Amazon at $220bn and explicitly short of capacity even so.

The week of 3 August 2026 introduced a distinction the desk had been collapsing. Capex is not one signal — it matters whether it is funded. [[googl]] raised to $195-205bn against cloud revenue up 82%, and entered Core coverage. [[meta]] raised its floor $10bn and missed EPS badly, and was stepped to watch. Part of the increase across the group is memory cost inflation rather than incremental compute units, so the headline dollars overstate the unit demand reaching suppliers.

The second-order observation from the same week: the payers rallied while the suppliers fell. Owning both ends of the trade is no longer the same position.

pages.title: Materials & Packaging
pages.note:
A lighter-touch, picks-and-shovels research theme sitting upstream of the [[fabs]] and [[advanced-packaging]] layers. [[aleabitoreddit]] views AEHR ([[aehr]])'s ~100% rally as largely priced in absent a new catalyst; LPKF ([[lpk-de]]) is his recurring bullish idea on a glass-core substrate near-monopoly — a bridge into the [[glass]] theme — with a stated multi-billion factory ambition; Soitec ([[soi-pa]]) rounds out the specialty-materials group.

These are second-derivative plays: they win if the [[memory]], [[photonics]] and packaging build-outs they supply keep scaling.

pages.title: AI Memory
pages.note:
The [[hbm]] memory upcycle is a high-conviction supply theme, and it got a clean real-world stress test in July 2026: Samsung pre-announced record Q2 operating profit up ~1,800% Y/Y — on his telling the most profitable quarter in the world — and the stock still fell ~7% after a +150% YTD run. [[aleabitoreddit]] reads that as priced-to-perfection profit-taking, not a fundamentals break, and notes the same Samsung print was the actual trigger for the broader chip rout.

[[mu]] is the liquid US expression of the DRAM/HBM cycle; [[sndk]] the NAND leg; [[axti]] the upstream substrate/materials feed (torque he also pairs with the [[photonics]] sleeve); [[rpi]] rounds out the group. The through-line is [[hbm]] scarcity — stacked memory bonded next to the GPU is the scarcest ingredient in every accelerator the [[hyperscalers]] are buying.

The 16 Jul 2026 review made memory the week's headline: TrendForce confirmed 13-18% server-DRAM contract hikes for Q3 with Samsung seeking 20%, [[mu]] disclosed 16+ long-term agreements, and [[sndk]]'s supply deal with [[meta]] was confirmed — while memory equities sold off into all of it. The desk opened SNDK coverage on that disconnect. The structural nuance worth keeping: SK Hynix reportedly scrapped LTA price caps while Micron kept ceilings-and-floors, so the same upcycle is captured very differently across the complex.

On 17 Aug 2026 the desk finally split the theme in two and added the DRAM leg through [[mu]], having held only NAND for a month. The correction worth remembering: treating "memory" as one bottleneck meant owning the loose half of it while the tight half compounded. The two markets are now held separately and sized together.

pages.title: Neoclouds
pages.note:
The neocloud sleeve holds [[nbis]] and, from 3 August 2026, [[iren]] — companies that contract power and capacity ahead of demand and convert it into annualised run-rate. The bet is that compute scarcity persists long enough for capacity secured today to be revenue two to four quarters out.

The week of 3 August 2026 clarified what risk this sleeve actually carries, and it is not demand. Nebius reported $399.0m of quarterly revenue against a $3-3.4bn full-year target, with capex plans an order of magnitude above revenue; IREN revised its ARR target above $4bn with Microsoft, Nvidia, Perplexity and Figure named as customers, but with less disclosure behind it. Both are financing stories wearing compute stories' clothes, and both were placed on watch.

Contracted ARR is not funded capacity. Until a second-half revenue step-up shows up on schedule, doubling this sleeve is a sizing decision rather than a reason to add a second correlated name.

pages.title: Networking
pages.note:
The switching and custom-silicon layer that moves data between accelerators. [[aleabitoreddit]]'s [[mrvl]] thread stays sentiment-first — every drop reminds him of Jensen's 'next $1T company' comment — and this week he formalized a half-serious 'conspiracy theory' that [[nvda]] quietly supports the ASIC challengers (Marvell, MediaTek, AlChip) chipping at [[avgo]]'s custom-silicon share.

[[avgo]] is the incumbent custom-silicon giant; [[mrvl]] the challenger he watches most; [[nok]] a peripheral networking name. The layer overlaps the [[photonics]] story where switching meets optics ([[cpo]]).

pages.title: Photonics
pages.note:
The theme the desk is built around: lasers, transceivers and the substrates beneath them, feeding the optical interconnect that co-packaged optics makes load-bearing.

August 2026 was the month the theme stopped being a narrative and started producing filed numbers. [[lite]] reported revenue up 109% year over year and crossed 50% non-GAAP gross margin a quarter early. [[cohr]] posted a record $2.05B quarter with datacom at 79% of revenue and six-inch indium phosphide capacity doubled ahead of plan. [[aaoi]] printed a fifth consecutive record quarter and returned to profit. The rotation the analyst describes is visible in the results, not only in the tape.

Two things the desk now reads differently. First, the margin ladder inside the layer is enormous and is the cleanest sorting mechanism available: [[mtsi]] guides 60-61%, [[lite]] just above 50%, [[cohr]] 39.5-41.5%, [[aaoi]] 29-30.5%. Content sold into the module earns roughly double what assembling the module earns. Second, Lumentum crossing its margin target early suggests the laser constraint is a merchant-supply problem rather than an industry yield problem — which is more bullish for the integrated names and less bullish for the small merchant suppliers the analyst prefers.

The discipline this theme needs is separating what is reported from what is modelled, because the two look alike when read quickly. Reported: Lumentum's guidance, Coherent's segment mix, AOI's margins, and the substrate reservation deposits at [[axti]]. Modelled: Sivers' capacity revenue figure at [[sive]], AOI's roughly $485M implied fourth quarter, and every read-through built on the proposed United States restriction on Chinese transceivers, which remains a draft rule.

pages.title: Robotics
pages.note:
Physical-AI is a high-conviction, high-euphoria theme — and one [[aleabitoreddit]]'s own posts became a case study in the anchoring psychology he critiques. His frame: Agility ([[ccxi]], becoming AGLT) is the purest US mass-production humanoid play via the Amazon/MercadoLibre supply chains, going public via SPAC to give retail access 'before it gets big.'

[[ccxi]] is the humanoid pure-play; [[aeva]] the lidar/perception supplier; [[tsla]] the mega-cap Optimus optionality. The desk treats the group as the most sentiment-driven corner of the map — real end-demand, but valuations running on narrative.

pages.title: AAOI · Applied Optoelectronics
pages.note:
Applied Optoelectronics is the high-beta datacom optics position in the book — the name whose valuation case has always rested on a forward revenue rate rather than current earnings. The 800G ramp itself is real and company-confirmed: Q1 revenue was a record $151.1m, up 51%, with Q2 shipments guided at nearly four times Q1 levels.

On 3 August 2026 the desk stepped the stance from accumulate to watch. The $471m monthly rate anchoring the bull case — about $5.6bn annualised from H2 2027 — is roughly five times the run-rate management guides to, with Q2 at $180-198m and the full year around $1.1bn. It circulates in the [[photonics]] discussion as though it were the company's own estimate. Q2 is also guided to non-GAAP EPS between -$0.03 and +$0.03, so the 'one times forward revenue' cheapness describes a top line that currently earns nothing.

The trigger back to accumulate is management guiding toward the rate the thesis assumes, or a named CPO customer with committed volume — see [[amd]], where that read-through is still inference rather than schedule.

pages.title: AXTI · AXT Inc
pages.note:
AXT sells the wafer everything else in [[photonics]] is grown on: indium phosphide and gallium arsenide compound substrates, the layer beneath the lasers at [[lite]], [[sive]] and [[aaoi]].

This is the desk's best-evidenced position in the stack, and the reason is unusual for this book. Almost every number carrying the photonics theme is modelled — Sivers' capacity revenue is a projection, AOI's 2028 external-light-source figure is a unit plan times an assumed price, Lumentum's CPO ramp is a dated statement about 2027. AXT's is not: Lumentum signed a long-term agreement with a $43.5M capacity reservation deposit, and Coherent signed earlier with $22.3M. Customers do not prepay for capacity they are unsure they will need, which makes these agreements evidence about the whole theme rather than just this company.

Two housekeeping notes. The desk dropped coverage of this name on 3 August and restored it on 12 August — the LTAs were already public at the time of the drop, so that was a miss rather than a change of facts. And the store currently files AXT under [[memory]], which is wrong: it sells compound substrate material, not memory, and the categorisation should move before it distorts the map or the theme digests.

pages.title: CCXI · Agility Robotics
pages.note:
Agility rotated off the desk's verdict roster in the 22 Jul 2026 review — zero new theses in a crash-dominated week let its priority score slip below the top-15 line, and a watch stance carries no sticky holdover protection. Nothing changed in the underlying story: the IBK actuator-capacity framing, the SPAC-structure caution, and the funded-Amazon-deployment upgrade trigger all stand exactly as the last verdict left them, and the [[robotics]] theme digest still carries the thesis.

The name re-enters coverage the same way it left — on score. A robotics news cycle or a dedicated post from [[aleabitoreddit]] would do it; the operator can also re-add it by request, as [[mu]] once was.

pages.title: GOOGL · Alphabet
pages.note:
Alphabet joined the verdict roster in the 16 Jul 2026 review on tier math alone — and the desk verdict says so: every mention in the corpus is contextual, never a mispricing argument. [[aleabitoreddit]] uses Google as the demand gauge of the AI buildout: the compute-constrained hyperscaler, the party that cut Meta off and taught the industry the cost of renting, and (this week) the counterfactual he believes pushed $AAPL toward AI-chip acquisitions. Watch stance; the upgrade trigger is a dedicated TPU-supply-chain thesis with named suppliers.

Rotated off the verdict roster in the 22 Jul 2026 review, one week after entering: the contextual mentions decayed and [[intc]] took the tier-math slot with the same context-name treatment. The demand-gauge framing survives the rotation — the desk still reads his Google mentions as evidence of structural compute hunger, just without a standing verdict attached.

pages.title: INTC · Intel Corporation
pages.note:
Intel entered the verdict roster in the 22 Jul 2026 review on tier math — crash-week mention volume, not a dedicated thesis. The desk's memo is blunt about the distinction: the corpus uses Intel as an instrument, not an idea. Its CEO's line that there is 'no relief in memory supply or pricing until at least 2028' is load-bearing evidence in the [[memory]] shortage case that anchors the [[mu]] and [[sndk]] positions, and 'INTC to LITE' is the span of [[aleabitoreddit]]'s market-bottom gauge for the whole semis complex.

The precedent is [[googl]], which entered the same way in the 16 Jul review and rotated off a week later when its contextual mentions decayed. Expect the same here unless a dedicated Intel thesis appears — foundry wins, advanced-packaging exposure, or CPO-adjacent capacity would make it analyzable inside this workflow. Until then the stance is watch, explicitly as a context name.

pages.title: LITE · Lumentum Holdings
pages.note:
Lumentum is the liquid, reported way to own the laser bottleneck that [[photonics]] is built on — the place where the theme shows up in guidance rather than in a model.

The desk moved it twice in three days in August 2026, and the second move was an admission. It was cut to wait on 10 August on one stated condition: an in-line print with unchanged capacity commentary. The 11 August result was the opposite — revenue up 109% year over year, guidance raised, and the operating-margin target reached more than a quarter early — so the call was restored on 12 August. Worth remembering as a case of trimming into a known event that was one day away.

The nuance the feed skips: the beat is current datacom optics. Management places the ultra-high-power laser and co-packaged optics ramp in the second half of calendar 2027, which is Lumentum's fiscal 2028, so no CPO revenue sits in these numbers. The confirming evidence is one floor down at [[axti]], where Lumentum prepaid a $43.5M deposit to reserve indium phosphide substrate capacity — a customer putting cash behind the volumes it expects to need.

pages.title: LPK.DE · LPKF Laser & Electronics
pages.note:
Re-categorised from [[materials]] into [[glass]] on 17 Aug 2026 and given its first desk verdict the same week — wait, no position. LPKF sells the LIDE laser systems that structure glass, the tooling a substrate maker buys before it can produce anything.

The timing of the initiation is unhelpful and worth recording honestly. The most recent thesis in the file is [[aleabitoreddit]] reporting a delay in his own theme: Samsung Electro-Mechanics pushing its glass-substrate investment out on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations, revising start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back. For an equipment supplier a customer's slip moves the revenue event with it, and there is no partial credit — the tool order lands before the line runs.

Sixteen accumulated mentions is what put it in Core. That is attention gathered over months rather than conviction expressed this week, and being the second name in a near-empty layer flatters the rank further. The entry trigger is a disclosed LIDE order from a named customer with a delivery year attached.

pages.title: META · Meta Platforms
pages.note:
Meta sits in this book as the payer rather than the product — held to validate that the capex funding the [[photonics]] and [[memory]] supply chain is genuinely being spent. On that narrow question it delivered: 2026 guidance of $130-145bn, with the low end rising $10bn in a single quarter.

On 3 August 2026 the desk stepped the stance from accumulate to watch. Q2 EPS was $6.18 against roughly $7.14 expected, on $60.8bn of revenue and $31.1bn of quarterly capex, and the shares fell about 8%. The desk's own weekly recap carried the capex number and dropped the miss, which is the bias worth naming: a supply-chain lens reads hyperscaler capex as a demand signal and stops reading there.

The conclusion is not that the supplier thesis broke. It is that holding Meta and holding Meta's suppliers have become opposite expressions of one view — the equity is being derated for the spending that creates the read-through — and this desk already owns the supply side. Compare [[googl]], where the same spend is visibly funded by an accelerating cloud business.

pages.title: MTSI · MACOM Technology Solutions
pages.note:
Entered Core coverage 17 Aug 2026 on the thinnest analyst attention on the roster — eleven mentions — and the strongest operating numbers in it. Fiscal Q3 revenue $342.2M, up 35.8% year on year, fiscal Q4 guided to $415-425M on a record 1.6 book-to-bill, with adjusted gross margin guided to 60-61%.

That margin is the whole case. Within [[photonics]], [[aaoi]] guides Q3 gross margin to 29-30.5%, [[cohr]] to 39.5-41.5%, and [[lite]] to just above 50%. MACOM sits above all of them because it sells the analog and photonic content inside a module rather than assembling the module — a structurally different business wearing the same theme.

[[aleabitoreddit]] frames it through indium phosphide security: long-term epiwafer agreements and a stake in [[iqe]]. The desk could not find a primary filing confirming the stake size or the terms, so that leg is carried as unverified and counts for nothing in the verdict. Initiated small; the second tranche waits on the fiscal Q4 print.

pages.title: MU · Micron Technology
pages.note:
The desk's DRAM and HBM leg, opened 17 Aug 2026 after two passes declining it. The earlier reasoning — that a cycle where the seller sets the price is the wrong moment to underwrite a multiple — was reversed on two facts. Scale: the last reported quarter put revenue at $41.46B against $9.30B a year earlier, with data centre alone above $25B, an annualised run-rate over $100B. And market: [[sndk]] expresses NAND, while the structural shortage is in DRAM and HBM, where 3Q26 server contract prices rise 13-18% quarter on quarter under long-term agreements and 2027 HBM contract prices are expected multiples higher against RDIMM bit supply growing only 15-20%.

The distinction between the two memory legs matters and is easy to lose. [[aleabitoreddit]] posts the [[memory]] bottleneck as a single undifferentiated theme; it is two markets tightening for different reasons, and only one of them was in the book before this week. They will still correlate hard in a drawdown, so combined memory weight — not either position alone — is what gets sized.

The falsifier is deliberately not a demand miss. It is the first quarter long-term agreement pricing stops rising.

pages.title: NBIS · Nebius Group
pages.note:
Nebius is the [[neoclouds]] position — the way to own AI compute demand without owning a hyperscaler or a chip designer. The operating execution is visible and on schedule: up to 1.2GW of power and land secured for an owned Pennsylvania site, and more than 3GW expected under contract by year-end. For a neocloud, energised capacity is the binding constraint and it is being cleared ahead of the revenue.

On 3 August 2026 the desk stepped the stance from accumulate to watch. Q1 revenue was $399.0m, annualising near $1.6bn against a full-year target of $3-3.4bn, so almost the entire guide sits in the second half. Capex plans run an order of magnitude above revenue, which makes the terms of the next capital raise a larger determinant of the equity return than GPU demand is.

Accumulate implied the risk being underwritten was demand. It is not — it is financing. Q2 results on 12 August are the next test. [[iren]] entered coverage the same week with better counterparties and the same unresolved funding question.

pages.title: NVDA · NVIDIA Corporation
pages.note:
NVIDIA is the gravitational center of this entire map rather than a stock pick. [[aleabitoreddit]] — and this desk — treat the edge as the layers beneath it: the [[photonics]], [[memory]] and [[fabs]] suppliers whose fortunes are levered to NVIDIA demand but priced far less efficiently.

This week NVDA appeared mainly as collateral in the narrative war (SemiAnalysis supply-chain bear posts) and in the Hesai lidar-scrutiny story. Desk stance is **watch**: express the thesis through the suppliers the map surfaces, and hold NVDA as a separate core-portfolio decision outside this workflow. It anchors the [[accelerators]] theme alongside [[amd]] and [[arm]].

pages.title: SIVE · Sivers Semiconductors
pages.note:
Sivers Semiconductors is [[aleabitoreddit]]'s single highest-conviction name and the highest-torque bet in the [[photonics]] sleeve — the InP laser supplier positioned at the chokepoint if co-packaged optics displaces pluggable modules. The structural argument is genuinely strong: Sivers and [[lite]] were the only two public laser suppliers named in the CPO programme that drew a $300m US award to [[gfs]].

On 3 August 2026 the desk stepped the stance from accumulate to watch. The reason is not the drawdown — it is that outside research put company numbers against the story for the first time and they point the other way. Q1 net sales were SEK 61.9m, down 22% year on year, and the $799m figure quoted as evidence is an opportunity pipeline rather than backlog. The [[poet]] wording change read as a material timeline upgrade resolves, in the only citable partnership language, to production readiness by end of 2026 — a milestone, not an order.

The falsifier is dated and close: the Q2 interim report on 27 August 2026. Existing tranches stand; new size waits for that print.

pages.title: SNDK · SanDisk
pages.note:
SanDisk entered desk coverage in the 16 Jul 2026 weekly review as the expression of the [[memory]] repricing — the week the story hardened from price-hike headlines into contracts, with the $META long-term agreement confirmed and an [[aehr]] NAND burn-in benchmark the analyst reads as SanDisk. Notably, [[aleabitoreddit]] has never written a dedicated SNDK thesis; the desk's accumulate stance rests on a mosaic of his memory-macro posts plus third-party verification (TrendForce, Jefferies), which the coverage memo flags openly.

The desk's caveat is the LTA cut-both-ways problem: long-term agreements guarantee volume but can cap price capture, and SanDisk's terms are undisclosed — the single most decision-relevant unknown on the name.

pages.title: TSLA · Tesla Inc
pages.note:
Tesla sits in this book for one reason — Optimus as a humanoid programme pulling on the same [[robotics]] and AI-compute supply chain — and it is the clearest example the desk has of a scoring artefact.

In August 2026 it ranked thirteenth by priority score on 19 mentions, which put it inside verdict coverage. Reading the underlying posts dissolves that: nearly every mention is an incidental name-drop inside a multi-ticker recap, one carrying twelve symbols. The substantive references amount to an Optimus quote lifted from the earnings transcript and an unverified third-party claim about polysilicon equipment contracts that the analyst prefaces by saying he is not familiar with the supply chain. The score is measuring the analyst's posting format, not his conviction.

Recorded at pass on 12 August specifically so it stops presenting as a top-15 idea. It is worth keeping as a live reminder that mention-weighted attention scores reward list-posts, and that the [[aleabitoreddit]] feed contains a lot of them.

pages.title: TSM · Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co
pages.note:
[[tsm]] was upgraded to accumulate this week, and it is a deliberate disagreement with [[aleabitoreddit]], who treats the foundry as scenery — everything is built there, so it carries no edge. That was right while the small suppliers were cheap. After a week in which [[aaoi]] rose about 77%, [[cohr]] 71%, [[sive]] 50% and [[lite]] 48%, the supplier book is priced for the shortage while TSMC is down about 7% on the month with first-half revenue up 35.6% and June alone up 67.9%.

It is also the only name in the book whose demand curve can be checked every thirty days rather than every quarter, and it carries none of the qualification, dilution or single-customer risk that the small caps do. The offsetting caution is that advanced packaging is easing rather than tightening — industry reporting has the CoWoS supply-demand gap narrowing from roughly 20% to 10% by end-2026 — so the bottleneck this layer owns is migrating upstream into [[photonics]] and substrates. The position is ballast, sized like [[jbl]], not a bet on the squeeze.

pages.title: XFAB · X-FAB Silicon Foundries
pages.note:
X-FAB is a specialty foundry that carries two stacked theses. The value leg: Kepler's upgrade calls it the cheapest specialty foundry at 4.8x 2027 EV/EBITDA versus a ~14.5x peer median, with Melexis demand strengthening. The free option: its 'photonixfab' silicon-photonics ([[siph]]) line, which [[aleabitoreddit]] thinks the market is not pricing at all.

That [[siph]] leg is why it lives on the [[photonics]] page rather than with the [[fabs]]. Desk stance is **accumulate** — the value floor justifies a real starter position, the photonics upside is the kicker — tempered by European-listing illiquidity and specialty-foundry cyclicality, which argue for patience.

stats.definition: Assembling multiple dies (GPU + HBM) into one part — often the real bottleneck, not the fab.
A layer with so few capable suppliers that demand has nowhere else to go — where pricing power lives.
This desk's ranking: core = repeat, high-conviction mentions; watch = credible but thinner; radar = one-off name-drops.
Co-packaged optics — moving the optical connection onto the chip package itself; the next photonics wave.
High-bandwidth memory — stacked DRAM bonded next to the GPU; the scarcest ingredient in every accelerator.
A cloud built almost entirely of GPUs for rent, not a general-purpose hyperscaler.
Silicon photonics — making optical parts with chip fabs, so light replaces copper between GPUs.
